lines.text: Alright, J, let's take a look at this. The developer finally swapped out those old C-style printf statements for proper std::cout streams.
And the file handling is running cleanly through standard streams. The memory management is looking sharp.
Finally! Though I was a bit worried when they stripped out my full logo and left me with just these raw curly brackets {} as a hairclip.
But hey, as long as the dialogue data parses neatly into this JSON structure, I can't complain.
The curly brackets look clean. More importantly, look at how the Raylib window is rendering our text right now.
The state machine is incrementing the dialogue index perfectly every time the action key is pressed.
True, but watch the margins! If the text strings get too long, the text-wrapping logic needs to handle the line breaks dynamically.
We can't have our sentences clipping out of the UI container or cut awkwardly in half.
Don't worry, the modular design means the text wrapping is separated from the rendering loop.
It calculates the character limits before drawing the font textures. It's built to be robust.
Good. Because if my nested strings or arrays cause a buffer overflow in your modular backend, I am never letting you live it down.
Relax. It's a modern standard setup now. No leaks, no crashes—just clean, modular code.
Let's advance to the next line and see if the portrait textures swap correctly.
